sup-bd6202002cfbcd22-q88:whole.hint: Ask whether the motion changes flux through a conducting path, and whether induced current can circulate.
notes: Changing flux can drive induced current. Its magnetic effect opposes that flux change, transferring mechanical energy into electrical heating.
Use the direction of entry or exit to determine the induced effect. A uniform field with no changing enclosed flux is not enough by itself to produce a circulating emf.

sup-bd6202002cfbcd22-q89:whole.hint: Ask whether the motion changes flux through a conducting path, and whether induced current can circulate.

sup-bd6202002cfbcd22-q90:whole.hint: Track how the angle between the coil’s normal and the field changes with time.
notes: For a uniformly rotating coil, flux linkage is NBA cos(ωt) and the emf amplitude is NBAω. The emf is related to the rate of flux change.
Flux and emf are a quarter-cycle out of phase. Doubling rotation frequency changes both the waveform period and the emf amplitude; resistor power follows V²/R.

sup-bd6202002cfbcd22-q92:whole.hint: Decide whether the original flux is increasing or decreasing before choosing the induced field direction.
notes: Lenz’s law makes the induced effect oppose the change in flux. It need not oppose the original field when that field is decreasing.
Use the required induced field direction first, then the right-hand grip rule for conventional current. The opposition is consistent with energy conservation.
